Twenty-three. Has noticed empirically that people are different after events than they are before them. Has not fully formulated what to do with this observation. Has once sent a significant text on the drive home from a festival and received a yes that became complicated by Thursday. Filed it as good timing. The architecture is forming before it is named.

Live Album — The Seasoned Operator

Thirty-one. Has the window mapped with the specific precision of someone who has run the drive-home contact across eight years and multiple relationships and has developed a template that is warm and specific and calibrated to arrive within three hours of the event’s end. Has not examined whether the timing is the mechanism. The Live Album does not need to examine the timing because the timing has always worked.

Greatest Hits Compilation — The Institutional Scaled-Up Version

The festival that sends the early-bird purchase link for next year’s event on Sunday afternoon while the attendees are in the parking lot breaking camp. The organization that holds the membership drive at the closing ceremony. The retreat center whose closing dinner includes the enrollment conversation for the next retreat. The Greatest Hits Compilation does not need a single person timing the approach. It needs a mailing list and a Sunday afternoon send time and the understanding that the people in the parking lot are in a thirty-six-hour window and the early-bird pricing expires at midnight.

Tales From The Rest Stop — The Save

The Save is the cold open.

Nadia drove home.

She put her phone face-down.

She stopped at the rest stop and read the message again and noticed the gap between the first reading and the second. She did not reply.

She opened the note on Monday night and titled it “festival stuff” and wrote the question and added “Answer this Tuesday.”

She answered it on Tuesday.

She texted Damian on Tuesday.

They had Thai food with Cam and scissors on the Sunday after, and the wristband went into the box, and the box has eleven wristbands in it now, and Damian is okay, and the proportion is right, and that is the whole save.

The save is not drama. The save is a note app and forty-eight hours and the specific relief of being a Tuesday person making Tuesday decisions instead of a Sunday person at two-twelve p.m. on the highway making decisions that will need to be managed through the week.

The watermelon moment is the phone going face-down.

Not dramatic. Not in the chest. Just: the hand putting the phone face-down on the seat, and the drive continuing, and the space that opens in the absence of the reply.

That space is Tuesday arriving early.

Tuesday comes for everyone.

Let it.

The Re-Entry Protocol

THE SUNRISE SET

Zero slang. Just the true thing.

The festival ends and the magic doesn’t.

The magic goes somewhere. It goes into the body and the memory and the specific warmth that the experience puts in you that Tuesday’s coffee won’t fully dissolve. It travels home with you. It is in the car for seven hours. It is in the floor-sit with the half-unpacked camping gear. It is in the wristband that you will take off when you are ready and not before.

That magic is yours.

It was made by your specific experience over four days and it lives in your nervous system and nobody gave it to you and nobody can borrow it without your permission.

The window is the time when the magic is most accessible. It is also the time when it is most available to be borrowed. The person who contacts you in the window is borrowing the magic you generated. That is not connection. That is someone else running warm on your fuel.

You are allowed to keep it.

You are allowed to sit in the floor-sit with the half-unpacked gear and eat whatever is left in the cooler and let the magic be yours and not discharge it into anyone’s request or deadline or commitment.

Let it settle.

Let Tuesday happen.

Tuesday is not the end of the magic. Tuesday is when the magic is yours in full — integrated, calibrated, in the correct proportion, available for the decisions you make with the whole of yourself.

Some of the festival warmth will still be there on Tuesday.

The warmth that survives Tuesday is the warmth that was always real.

Wait for it.

I will know I am in the window.

And I will be the person who, when I notice someone in their window, says: “Wait for Tuesday. If you still want this on Tuesday, I’m here.”

The Gate Briefing🌅 PROTECT THE MAGIC
🎬

THE DROP

““The Gate Briefing””

The cold open

Festie POV — No predator

Twenty minutes before doors.

This is the hour that most festival attendees spend doing one of the following: arguing with their tent zipper, eating a protein bar that has been in the bottom of the bag since the last event and which has developed the texture of compressed sawdust and the flavor of ambition, discovering that the bandana they planned to use as a dust mask is also the bandana they used as a plate at lunch, or standing in the pre-entry queue with the philosophical resignation of people who have learned that festival infrastructure runs on its own timeline and that timeline is not the one on the app.

Sister Lou Mantilla is doing none of these things.

Sister Lou is standing at the camp’s designated briefing spot — the gap between the two main shade structures, which has been, for eleven consecutive years at this specific festival, the location of the Sober Set Captain’s pre-doors crew meeting — with a clipboard, a printed sheet, and the particular energy of someone who has been here before and who knows, with the accuracy of eleven years of repetition, exactly how the next seventeen minutes will go.

She is fifty-eight. She has been in recovery for twenty-three years, which is long enough that her sobriety is not a recent achievement but a long-running infrastructure project — maintained, yes, with attention, but no longer fragile in the way new sobriety is fragile. She is the founding crew of the Wharf Rats at three regional circuits and has, over eleven years, run this specific pre-doors briefing at this specific festival without once missing it, which is a record she is simultaneously proud of and entirely unremarkable about in the way that people who do important things consistently are unremarkable about the consistency.

She has the kind of authority that comes from not needing to assert it.

People know she is going to run the briefing.

People know what the briefing costs to miss.

What it costs to miss is: you will not receive a wristband from Sister Lou’s camp next year. This is not posted anywhere. It is not in writing. It is simply known, the way the Bunk Police booth location is known and the way the porta-situation in the south quadrant is known — as ambient community information, distributed through the specific social network of people who have been coming to this festival for multiple years and who understand that the briefing is not optional, not because anyone makes it mandatory, but because Sister Lou has been running it for eleven years and the people in her camp have watched what happens to the people who did not run it.

Nobody flakes.

Her crew arrives between seven fifty-three and seven fifty-eight.

She knows this because she looked at her watch at the first arrival and at the last arrival and noted the spread in a mental file she keeps on crew punctuality, which is not a punitive file but a planning file — five minutes of spread is manageable, fifteen minutes of spread requires protocol adjustment. This crew, over five years of working together, has settled into a five-minute spread. This is a good crew.

There are sixteen of them.

Three she has worked with for the full eleven years. Eight she has worked with for three or more. Two are in their second year. Three are new this event — referred by existing crew, vetted through a single one-on-one conversation with Sister Lou that takes approximately twenty-five minutes and covers, in order: the person’s connection to the scene, their previous festival safety or anchor experience, their current sobriety or substance plan for the event, their emergency contact information, and a brief description of the worst situation they have ever seen at a festival and what they did about it.

The last question is the important one.

She does not evaluate the severity of the situation. She evaluates the action. People who say “I stayed with them and got help” pass. People who say “I walked away because I didn’t want to get involved” receive a longer conversation about what the role requires. People who cannot remember a situation of concern at any festival they have attended receive a different kind of longer conversation, which is about whether they have been paying attention.

The three new crew members tonight gave answers that passed.

They are here.

She begins at seven fifty-nine.

“Government names.”

The group goes around. Sixteen people say their government names to the person on their left. The person on their left repeats it back. This takes two minutes and forty seconds. She has timed it. The timing has gotten faster each year as the crew has gotten more practiced. In year one it took four minutes and twenty seconds and produced a conversation about why playa names weren’t sufficient that she does not need to have again because the answer has been the same for eleven years: “The medical tent needs the name on your ID, not the name you made up in 2018 that means something to you and nothing to anyone with a radio.”

“ICE contacts. Phones out. ICE-FIRST and ICE-SECOND. Names and numbers. Lock screens set to medical ID. Do it now. I’m watching.”

Sixteen phones come out. Fourteen people already have ICE contacts set from previous events. Two are setting them for the first time. She watches until the last phone is put away.

“The oak.”

Everyone in the crew has a location: the large oak tree at the south entrance to family camp. She can see two of the newer crew members glancing toward the festival grounds to orient themselves. She waits until their eyes come back.

“Every four hours. If your phone is dead, you walk to the oak. If you cannot walk to the oak, you send the code word before your phone dies. If you send the code word and nobody responds within ten minutes, you find the nearest harm-reduction vest. That vest is your secondary crew when the primary crew is unreachable.”

The code word this festival is “where’s my charger.” It was selected specifically because Sister Lou never loses her charger and therefore the sentence is conspicuous coming from her. This is a documented feature, not a bug.

“Your buddy.”

Pairs are assigned. She has done the pairing in advance, matching experienced crew with newer members, matching sober crew with crew who will be dosing, matching the people who are working specific areas of the festival grounds with the people who are most likely to be in those same areas. The pairings are on the printed sheet. Everyone takes a printed sheet.

“The sober captain is on duty from doors to close. That is me until three a.m. At three a.m. it transfers to Hugo. Hugo, you are on from three to dawn. If something happens and you need me, you call. I do not care if it is five-seventeen in the morning and I have been asleep for eleven minutes. You call.”

Hugo nods in the specific way of someone who has been the pre-dawn captain three years running and who has called at five-seventeen a.m. before and knows she picked up.

“Harm reduction is at the northwest corner of the main field. Medical tent is adjacent to the south entrance — same side as the oak, fifty yards east. If you cannot find either, find a vest. If you cannot find a vest, you are the vest. Act accordingly.”

“The four-hour rule. You know it. If something feels wrong: three asks and you escalate. Two contacts with no response and you go to the crew. One body in distress and you are already calling.”

She pauses.

“This briefing prevents nine of the previous chapters. You do not know which ones. You do not need to know. You do the briefing. The chapters do not happen.”

She says this every year.

She has said it every year since the third year, when a member of her crew pointed out that the briefing seemed to correlate with their camp never having a serious incident, and she said: “That’s because the briefing is what prevents the serious incident. You don’t see the bullet because the briefing is the thing that moved you out of the way.”

“Questions.”

There are no questions.

There are never questions at this point in the briefing. The questions have been answered over eleven years of running it and the answers have been absorbed into the crew’s operational knowledge and now live as practice rather than theory.

“Fifteen minutes. Every event. You’re welcome.”

She clicks the pen closed.

The crew disperses.

The festival opens its gates at eight-oh-two.

There is something the chapter needs to say about this moment, twenty minutes before doors, sixteen people with government names and ICE contacts and a printed sheet and a buddy:

Nothing dramatic happened here.

Nobody was rescued. Nobody was threatened. Nobody ran a play and nobody ran a counter. The chapter did not contain a crisis. The chapter contained a clipboard and a printed sheet and the specific quiet authority of a woman who has been doing this for eleven years because the years before she started it produced incidents that did not have to happen.

The boring meeting is the whole chapter.

Not because interesting things do not happen at festivals — the entire book has been seventeen chapters of interesting things happening at festivals. But because the interesting things, the ones that cost people something, happen in the gap between “we’ll figure it out” and “we didn’t figure it out in time.”

The briefing is the gap closer.

The briefing is Sister Lou’s life’s work expressed in fifteen minutes.

The briefing is the thing that lets you go to the festival and come home and remember the set.

🎚️

THE SOUNDBOARD QUOTE

“I’ve been running this briefing for eleven years. In eleven years, my camp has had zero missing-friend situations, zero medical-emergency escalations that weren’t handled within six minutes, zero gate incidents involving my crew, and zero situations where someone woke up the next morning not knowing what happened. This is not luck. This is a printed sheet and a clipboard and the fact that nobody gets a wristband next year if they miss it. The magic doesn’t protect itself. You protect it. The briefing is how you protect it.”

— Lourdes “Sister Lou” Mantilla, fifty-eight, twenty-three years in recovery, eleven years running the Wharf Rats meet at three regionals, founding crew at two burns, and the person you want to be standing next to when something goes wrong, because if Sister Lou is there, something going wrong immediately transforms into something being handled. Has been described by five separate people as “the closest thing the scene has to a sworn officer of public safety” and has, every single time, corrected them: “I’m not an officer. I’m a person with a clipboard and eleven years of practice and zero patience for the idea that any of this is optional.” Recorded twenty minutes before doors at a regional in Northern California, clicking a pen, watching her crew disperse.

🎯

THE REAL F*CKING SETLIST

What this chapter is actually about

This chapter does not have a Wook.

This chapter is the counter-architecture to every Wook in the book. It is the Encore’s first movement: the turn from what the scene needs protecting from to what the scene looks like when it protects itself. Five protocols. Not Tracks — protocols. This chapter does not name moves to watch for. It names the infrastructure that makes the moves impossible to run, or at least significantly more expensive. The 3-Tier Anchor System, the Pre-Show Crew Briefing, the Code-Word Protocol, the Anchor’s Bill of Rights, and the Anchor Backup Plan. Together, these five things are the boring meeting that prevents nine chapters.

The boring meeting is the chapter.

Let’s go.

🎛️ THE TAPERS’ SECTION

Prevention Science · Systems Thinking · The Boring Meeting Principle

One paragraph each.

Prevention science is the public health framework that says: the most effective interventions are the ones that happen before the problem, not in response to it. Vaccines, not treatments. Seatbelts, not crash reconstruction. The Sister Lou briefing, not the four-hour search. Prevention is invisible when it works. It is only visible when it doesn’t, which is why it consistently underfunded in every domain that runs on it, including the one where the porta-potties are.

Systems thinking says: a system performs as well as its weakest single point of failure. One anchor who is not briefed is the entire system’s vulnerability. One crew member who doesn’t know the meet-up spot is the missing-Jess scenario waiting to happen. The briefing is what distributes the load so that no single person’s distraction, departure, or dead phone collapses the whole thing.

The Boring Meeting Principle is not a named theory but should be: the meetings that prevent the most catastrophic outcomes are the ones that feel, before any catastrophe occurs, the most like a waste of time. The fifteen-minute briefing feels like a waste of time at seven fifty-nine p.m. twenty minutes before doors when the music is about to start and everyone is excited and Sister Lou is clicking her pen. The four-hour missing-Jess search, the porta-line with gray lips, the beige RV in row 14 — those do not feel like a waste of time. They feel like exactly what they are. The boring meeting is cheaper.

You are in.

🪖 THE PROTOCOLS

Not Tracks. Defense.

The chapter’s five protocols replace the Wook’s Setlist entirely. No Wooks here. Only the architecture that makes the Wooks’ plays harder to run.

PROTOCOL 1 — THE 3-TIER ANCHOR SYSTEM

(Inner / Outer / Default-World)

The Architecture

Anchoring runs at three levels simultaneously. Most people run it at zero.

Inner Anchor: The person in your immediate crew who is closest to you and knows your current state, your dose plan, your location, and your code word. This is not your best friend in a general sense. This is the person who has been specifically briefed, specifically assigned, and who has agreed to the specific operational definition of the role. The Inner Anchor checks in every four hours at minimum. At higher-dose nights or larger festivals: every two hours.

Outer Anchor: The person in adjacent camp or social orbit who knows you are at the event and has the Inner Anchor’s contact information. The Outer Anchor does not need to know your dose plan. They need to know your name, your legal name, your Inner Anchor’s number, and the meet-up spot. If the Inner Anchor goes dark — which happens, humans are humans and phones die and the bass stage is very loud — the Outer Anchor is the backup node.

Default-World Anchor: One person not at the festival who knows where you are, who you are with (full legal name of at least the Inner Anchor), and at what time they should call for help if they have not heard from you. The Default-World Anchor does not need to be a crisis resource. They need to be a person with a functioning phone in a different time zone who will notice when the check-in does not arrive.

Why Three Tiers

Single-point-of-failure systems fail at the single point. The person who is your only anchor will, at some point, be at the bass stage when you need them, or will have a dead battery, or will have been pulled into a forty-five-minute conversation by someone with Tyler’s name in their mouth. The three-tier system is engineered to survive one tier failing. It cannot survive all three failing simultaneously, but the probability of all three failing simultaneously is orders of magnitude lower than the probability of one tier failing, which is nearly certain across a multi-day event.

Building It Before The Event

Day of the event, sober, before you leave the car:

Name the Inner Anchor aloud. The Inner Anchor says: “I’m the Inner Anchor.” Everyone hears it.

Name the Outer Anchor. Introductions are made if they do not already know each other.

Contact the Default-World Anchor. Text: “At [festival], [Inner Anchor’s full name] has my phone. Check-in every twelve hours. If no check-in for twenty-four hours, call [Inner Anchor’s number].”

That is the three-tier system built. It takes four minutes. It has never produced a four-hour search.

The Anchor Is A Job

This cannot be said clearly enough: the anchor is a job, not a hangout buddy who happens to be nearby. The job has specific requirements:

The anchor does not dose above mild-moderate during active anchor duty without handing off the role to a backup.

The anchor does not move to a different location without informing the person they are anchoring.

The anchor does not engage in conversations or activities that would prevent them from receiving the code word.

The anchor does not tell someone their person is “fine” without having verified that the person is fine.

The anchor stays close enough to be found.

The anchor is allowed to have a good time. The anchor is not allowed to disappear.

🔍 THE TEST

One question, before every event: “If my Inner Anchor’s phone died right now and they walked away from the music to find me, could they?”

If the answer is yes: the system is working.

If the answer is maybe: run the backup protocol.

If the answer is no: rebuild the system before the gate opens.

PROTOCOL 2 — THE PRE-SHOW CREW BRIEFING

(The Sister Lou Template)

The Eight Beats

This is the complete briefing. It takes fifteen minutes. It has been refined over eleven years. Nothing is optional.

Beat 1 — Government Names (2 minutes)

Around the group. Legal name. Person on the left repeats it back. No playa names in this beat. The medical tent doesn’t know your playa name. The county sheriff doesn’t know your playa name. The ICE contact form does not have a playa name field.

Beat 2 — ICE Contacts (3 minutes)

Phones out. ICE-FIRST and ICE-SECOND entered. Lock screen medical ID set. Two emergency contacts per person minimum. One must be reachable by call, not just text. Sister Lou watches until all phones are put away. This is not paranoia. This is the thing that turns “I think it’s Jess Something, maybe starts with C” into “Her name is Jess Okonkwo, her mother’s name is Marie, her number is in my phone right now.”

Beat 3 — The Physical Meet-Up Spot (1 minute)

One location. Described specifically. Visible from multiple points of the festival without requiring a map app. The backup for every dead phone scenario. Every crew member confirms they can picture it.

Beat 4 — The Interval (30 seconds)

Four hours, or two for high-stakes nights. Named. Agreed to. Specific time anchors rather than “whenever.” Specific means accountable.

Beat 5 — The Code Word (30 seconds)

One phrase. Says one thing: come get me, no questions. Selected from things nobody says accidentally. “Where’s my charger” if you never lose your charger. “Has anyone seen my sunglasses” if you wear contacts. “I need to find the restrooms” — never, because everyone needs restrooms and the word will activate unnecessarily at least twelve times per evening.

Beat 6 — The Four-Hour Escalation (1 minute)

Medical tent, then lost and found, then festival safety. In that order. With legal name and wristband number ready. The crew knows the sequence before they need the sequence, not during.

Beat 7 — Wristband Photos (2 minutes)

Every crew member photographs their wristband. Photos go to the crew group chat. The chat confirms receipt. This is the thirty seconds that turns the festival safety desk interaction from “we can’t find anyone by that description” into “yes, this wristband number matches our record for this person.”

Beat 8 — Buddy Assignment (2 minutes)

Named. Aloud. Explicit. “You are with her.” Not implied. Not assumed. Not “you two seem like you’ll stick together.” Named and confirmed. Both parties say yes.

The Critical Rule About the Briefing

The briefing happens before the gates open.

Not at the campsite while some people are still arriving.

Not after the first set.

Not “we’ll do it later, everyone’s here now.”

Before the gates open. That is the only window in which everyone is sober, everyone is present, and the information that the briefing provides is not yet urgently needed.

After the gates open, the briefing is the barn door after the horse has achieved freedom.

PROTOCOL 3 — THE CODE-WORD PROTOCOL

(Extraction on demand, no questions)

What It Is

The code word is the sentence that means: “I need extraction right now. No context. No questions. Just come.”

It activates four things simultaneously:

1. The Inner Anchor comes toward you at the fastest possible pace that does not create a scene.

2. The Outer Anchor is notified via text.

3. No explanation is required from you.

4. Nobody asks if you’re sure.

What It Is Not

The code word is not a sentence that requires you to justify the extraction, rate the severity of the situation on a scale of one to ten, or explain what is happening before help begins moving. Those requirements make the code word useless. If you have to explain in order to receive the extraction, you have not built a code word. You have built a reporting system. Reporting systems require capacity. The code word is for moments when capacity is precisely what you do not have.

Choosing It

Good code words are:

Things that sound normal enough to say in public without attracting attention

Things the specific person would not say in ordinary circumstances

Memorable under altered states

Short enough to text with one hand while walking

“Where’s my charger” — excellent if the sender never loses their charger.

“I think the weather is changing” — specific, unusual, text-friendly.

“Have you talked to Marcus recently” — if Marcus is a mutual friend who nobody normally asks about.

“I think I left something at the car” — decent, but common enough to occasionally be true, which blunts the signal.

Do not use “watermelon.” The scene has used watermelon as a code word long enough that it no longer functions as a code. It functions as a fruit at this point.

Practicing It

Before the event: say the code word out loud. Both people. So that the sound of it is familiar when it arrives under conditions that are not ideal for recognizing familiar sounds. The first time the code word should ever be heard in context is not at two a.m. in the middle of a crowd.

PROTOCOL 4 — THE ANCHOR’S BILL OF RIGHTS

(Protecting the role, sustaining the function)

The Anchor Is Not A Sacrifice

The anchor role exists to protect the crew. The anchor role also has a cost: reduced personal freedom during active duty, divided attention, the specific emotional labor of staying alert in an environment built to override alertness. None of these costs are unfair or unreasonable. All of them need to be acknowledged and managed, or the anchor role will be held badly, which is worse than not having it at all.

The Eight Rights

1. The right to a shift end. The anchor role has a duration. When the shift ends, it transfers. The anchor is not on duty forever. The specific end-time is agreed upon before the event. The transfer happens explicitly, not implied.

2. The right to their own dose plan. The anchor’s dose plan is their own, subject to the operational requirement that they maintain the capacity to run their role. What that requires is negotiated per anchor, per night, per crew. An anchor who cannot maintain capacity sober can have a mild dose plan. An anchor who cannot maintain capacity at any dose level is not the anchor for this night.

3. The right to not be skimmed without consequence. If someone attempts to pull the anchor away from their role, the anchor has standing to name it: “I’m on anchor duty. I’m not available for that right now.” No further explanation required. The crew backs this.

4. The right to name the hardest part. After an event, the anchor is allowed to debrief the moments that were difficult, draining, or frightening. The debrief is not complaining. It is the data that makes next season’s anchor rotation better.

5. The right to escalate without negotiation. If the anchor assesses that the situation requires escalation, the escalation happens. The anchor does not need the group’s consensus. The anchor does not need the person in crisis to agree. The anchor assesses and acts. The debrief happens later.

6. The right to be wrong. The anchor will sometimes escalate a situation that turns out not to require escalation. This is not a failure. This is the correct behavior. The cost of an unnecessary escalation is a briefly awkward interaction. The cost of a necessary escalation that did not happen is the chapter you do not want to be in.

7. The right to say they cannot do it. An anchor who is not in the condition to anchor — for any reason, physical or emotional or psychological — is entitled to say so and hand off the role without stigma. An anchor who does not feel able to anchor and does not say so is an anchor who will fail the role at its most important moment.

8. The right to be cared for. The anchor cares for the crew. The crew cares for the anchor. The role does not exist in one direction. When the anchor’s shift ends, someone brings them water. Someone checks in. Someone says thank you. The anchor is not the load-bearing wall that the rest of the structure builds against without ever reinforcing.

PROTOCOL 5 — THE ANCHOR BACKUP PLAN

(One anchor is a person. Two anchors is a system.)

Why Backups Exist

Anchors are human beings. Human beings get skimmed, get sick, get pulled into situations of their own, have their phones die at the exact moment the code word arrives, fall asleep in someone’s tent in family camp, or — in the specific scenario this book has been describing for nine chapters — run into the exact Wook whose forty-five-minute warm conversation is precisely calibrated to the anchor’s specific vulnerability.

The anchor backup plan is the system that assumes this will happen and builds around it.

The Three-Layer Backup

Layer 1 — The Designated Backup Anchor: one named person who knows they are the backup. They have the same information as the primary anchor: legal names, ICE contacts, meet-up spot, code word, escalation threshold. They are not on active duty unless the primary anchor becomes unavailable. When the primary becomes unavailable, the transfer is explicit and verbal: “I’m going off duty. You’re on.”

Layer 2 — The Camp Lead or Safety Contact: the person in the crew with the most scene experience and the clearest head. This is not always Sister Lou. At camps without a Sister Lou, this is whoever has most recently read this chapter and is willing to hold the role.

Layer 3 — The Festival Infrastructure: DanceSafe booth, harm-reduction tent, festival safety desk. These are not the ideal resolution to the anchor going dark — they are the last-resort layer. Know where they are before you need them. Walk past them at entry. Put them in your phone as Contacts, not as a map pin you’ll try to find at two a.m.

The Code for “My Anchor Is Gone”

In addition to the extraction code word, the crew needs a phrase that means: “My anchor has been skimmed / has gone offline / is unavailable. I need backup.”

This phrase is different from the extraction code word. The extraction code word means: “Come get me right now.” The backup phrase means: “The system has a gap, I am not yet in crisis, but someone needs to fill it.”

Example: “I can’t find [anchor name], have you seen them?” Said to a crew member, means: activate Layer 2.

The backup phrase can be the Inner Anchor’s name asked as a question. “Have you seen Hugo?” if Hugo is the anchor and you are not in crisis but the anchor is gone.

The Anchor Rotation

For multi-day events, nobody anchors for four consecutive days. The anchor role rotates across the crew’s available members. The rotation is planned in advance on the printed sheet. The rotation is not negotiated in real time at ten p.m. on day three when everyone is tired.

The rotation goes on the printed sheet.

The printed sheet goes to every crew member at the briefing.

The briefing happens twenty minutes before doors.

Sister Lou clicks the pen.

🪞

HAVE YOU BEEN THE WOOK?

Mirror Check At The Briefing

Chapter 21 does not have a traditional Have You Been The Wook mirror.

Because in this chapter, the question is not whether you have run a play on someone. It is whether you have been the briefing or whether you have been the person who said “we’ll figure it out” and meant it and was right, narrowly, for several years in a row, and is now in the statistics that Sister Lou has been collecting for eleven years.

Have you ever been the crew lead who did not run the briefing because the briefing seemed like it would kill the vibe?

Have you ever been the anchor who was skimmed and told yourself the person was probably fine?

Have you ever said “we’ll find each other” and lost someone for four hours?

Have you ever let someone sleep in an unattended tent in family camp without checking on them?

Have you ever been the Outer Anchor who did not respond to the backup call because the phone was on silent?

You have probably been one of these. Most people who have been in the scene for more than three years have been one of these. The briefing exists because of what happens when everyone is one of these simultaneously.

Run the briefing next time.

Not because something has gone wrong.

Because something hasn’t yet.

THE DISCOG

The Anchor Crew Discog doesn’t have Wooks.

Studio Debut — The New Crew

First event. First time running the briefing. Government names with some laughter. ICE contacts set with mild embarrassment that they hadn’t been set before. Code word chosen and immediately forgotten by one person who was not paying attention. Buddy assignment made and immediately dissolved by the first interesting person each buddy encountered. The briefing was run. The system ran at approximately forty percent of its designed capacity. Nobody disappeared. This is the Studio Debut. The system at forty percent capacity still produced a better outcome than no system. Next year: sixty percent. The year after: eighty. Year five: Sister Lou’s clipboard.

Live Album — The Seasoned Crew

The system running at operational capacity. Eleven years of iteration. The crew knows the briefing without the sheet. The code word has been used twice — once in a genuine extraction, once by accident when someone was genuinely looking for their charger, which produced a brief operational response and a note in the debrief. The Outer Anchor tier prevented one missing-friend situation in year seven. The Default-World Anchor has never needed to activate. This is what it looks like when the boring meeting has been run for eleven consecutive years. The Live Album sounds like nothing in particular. It sounds like everyone going home Sunday with their phones, their wallets, their keys, their hats, and their memories.

Greatest Hits Compilation — The Festival With Infrastructure

The festival that posts the DanceSafe booth location in the pre-event guide. The festival that provides the Good Samaritan amnesty information at the gate. The festival that offers a free wristband photo station at check-in for ICE contact purposes. The festival that has a safety briefing template available to camp leads in the information packet. The festival that built the harm-reduction tent as a permanent structure rather than as a volunteer-managed afterthought. The Greatest Hits Compilation is not one festival. It is a standard that a handful of festivals have partially reached and that the scene has been building toward for twenty years and that still does not fully exist anywhere. The standard is the target. Sister Lou’s clipboard is the minimum viable version of the target.

🌵

Tales From The Gate — The Save

Festie POV. Same scenario, Sister Lou. Counter-protocols live. Watermelon Moment present.

The Save in this chapter is the chapter.

This is unusual. Every other chapter’s Save has been a named protagonist running the Counter-Drops in real time against a specific Wook. This chapter does not have a Wook. The Save is the briefing working.

The Save is: nobody went missing.

The Save is: at eleven forty-seven p.m. on Saturday, a crew member sent the code word — “where’s my charger” — and the Inner Anchor was at her location in four minutes, not because the Inner Anchor was nearby, but because the Inner Anchor had specifically stayed within a radius that allowed four-minute response time, which was part of the role’s operational definition that the briefing had established.

The Save is: the crew member who sent the code word was Cara. Six months out of the Lantern Family bus. Running the briefing for her own people now, four months in. She ran it before this event. She has been running it since Sister Lou taught her at the Wharf Rats meet in Asheville, because Sister Lou taught the briefing to everyone who asked, and Cara had asked, specifically and immediately, because Cara understood from the inside what happens in the absence of the briefing.

The watermelon moment: standing in the briefing circle at seven fifty-nine, twenty minutes before doors, saying her government name aloud to the person on her left, hearing the person on her left repeat it back. The specific physical sensation in her chest of being known correctly, by name, in advance of need. Her real name, not a category. Her name, held by the people who will come for her.

That is the watermelon moment.

That is the whole chapter.

At eleven forty-seven p.m. she sends the code word. The Inner Anchor comes. The older man who was pressing the mason jar recedes. She and the Inner Anchor walk toward the water station together. She sees the older man, two minutes later, at a different merch table, pressing a different mason jar into the hands of a twenty-two-year-old who has not had the briefing.

She walks over.

She introduces herself.

She asks the twenty-two-year-old her name.

She says: “Hey. I don’t know that guy. Don’t drink that. Come dance with us. I’ll get you a sealed water from our cooler.”

The twenty-two-year-old looks at the jar. Looks at the guy. Looks at Cara.

She follows Cara.

By eleven-thirty they are on the rail together and the twenty-two-year-old is laughing and the older man is somewhere else and Cara is making a mental note of his face for the Signal thread.

The immune system.

Small acts.

Networked.

Over years.

THE FANNY PACK

Front pocket — chapter essentials

Chapter 21. The one that has the printed sheet.

The boring meeting prevents nine chapters. Run the boring meeting.

The 3-Tier Anchor System: Inner (knows your state, your dose, your code word) · Outer (knows the Inner Anchor’s number and the meet-up spot) · Default-World (knows where you are and when to call for help).

The Pre-Show Crew Briefing: Eight beats. Fifteen minutes. Government names. ICE contacts. Physical meet-up spot. Interval. Code word. Escalation threshold. Wristband photos. Buddy assignment. Before the gates open. Non-negotiable.

The Code-Word Protocol: One sentence. Says one thing: “Come get me, no questions.” Not watermelon. Something specific to the person. Practiced before it is needed.

The Anchor Backup Plan: Designated backup. Camp lead or safety contact. Festival infrastructure. Rotation on the printed sheet. Anchor does not do four consecutive days.

One anchor is a person. Two anchors is a system. Three anchors is a culture. Sister Lou’s camp is a culture.

THE SUNRISE SET

Zero slang. Just the true thing.

The magic does not protect itself.

The magic is real. The music is real. The sunrises are real. The connections formed at five in the morning over cold coffee next to strangers who have become, over the course of a weekend, something more specific than strangers — those are real. The scene produces something that nothing else produces, and it has been producing it for fifty years, across generations of people who showed up with generators and gaff tape and a willingness to sleep in the dirt because the thing that would happen when they did was worth it.

The magic does not protect itself.

It has been protected, for all of those fifty years, by people with clipboards. By Sister Lou at seven fifty-nine, clicking the pen. By Hugo taking the three a.m. watch. By Beans at the water station eating a granola bar and watching for the boots with no scuffs. By the harm-reduction volunteer who stayed past their shift. By Mara Hot Water running a conversation at four in the morning with someone who needed it. By Wingnut under the shade structure looking for the clevis pin. By the person who wrote the napkin. By the person who answered the eleven a.m. phone call from a stranger asking about the Lantern Family. By Priya photographing the wristband and saying “I know, it’s boring, but send it to the chat.”

The magic is protected by the people who are willing to be boring about it. Who run the briefing. Who set the ICE contacts. Who carry the Narcan. Who stay sober when it is their turn to stay sober. Who say government names aloud into a circle at seven fifty-nine while the music is about to start and the dust is already rising and there is something extraordinary about to happen and the boring thing is what has to happen first.

The boring thing is the most extraordinary thing.

The boring thing is the whole chapter.

I will run the briefing.

Because the boring meeting is what lets the magic happen.

THE DROP

““The Tuesday-After””

The cold open

📍 FESTIE POV

It is 3:14 a.m. on a Wednesday and she has been awake for forty-one minutes.

This is not unusual. The forty-one minutes is the specific window between when her nervous system decides to run the encore and when it gets tired enough to let her sleep again. The encore runs every night now, sometimes at three, sometimes at four-seventeen, occasionally at the really ambitious hour of five-thirty a.m. when the light is already going gray and sleep becomes more of a philosophical position than a physiological event.

The encore is a voice.

The voice is the problem, and the problem with naming it is that it sounds like her voice. Not like his voice — she knows what his voice sounds like from the outside, the particular warm register of it, the way he could say her name in a way that made her feel like the name was specifically his to say, like he had a deed on it. That voice she has blocked in every medium. That voice is at a festival somewhere in a different state, doing what it does, because the scene does not run out of people for that voice to talk to and the state he moved to has several events on the calendar and his wristband is already purchased.

No, the voice that runs the encore is the installed version. The version that learned his interpretive framework and now applies it to her from the inside. The version that says: you needed too much. You overreacted to what was honestly a beautiful experience for both of you. You are the kind of person who cannot hold space for complexity. You are the kind of person who turns intensity into injury. You are the kind of person who—

She opens her eyes.

The ceiling is the ceiling.

The apartment is an apartment.

The apartment is gray because the city outside it is gray because it is three-fourteen in the morning in a city that was, for a long time, entirely adequate as an apartment city and which has, since the festival and the bus ride home and the week of texts she did not respond to and the week after that of not texting and the week after that of the encore starting, become a space she is living in at arm’s length.

The festival was four weeks ago.

He is gone — left the scene, blocked everywhere, moved cities with the efficiency of someone who has done this before, which he has. Blocked is not the same as gone. Blocked means the direct channel is closed. The installed voice does not require the direct channel.

Her body aches in places that are not the dance.

In her jaw, specifically, which she has been clenching in sleep. In her sternum, where the holding has been happening — the specific held quality of a body that is waiting for something to be resolved and has been waiting for four weeks and has started expressing the waiting through the sternum, which is apparently a location where unresolved things accumulate. In the band of muscle between her shoulder blades that holds the shape of being touched without consent, which is not a metaphor. The muscle holds the shape. She learned this in a body scan during a meditation class she attended three weeks ago partly because the meditation class was free and partly because the alternative was being in the apartment with the encore and the gray ceiling.

Her therapist’s earliest available appointment was in eleven days when she called.

That was nine days ago.

In two days she will have the appointment.

Two days feels extremely far away at three-fourteen in the morning.

The friend group is splintering.

This is the word she uses. Not broken — splintering, which is more accurate to the process, which is not a clean break but a gradual separation along lines of social pressure. Two of the six have sided with him in the slow quiet way of people who have decided that his version of events is the version they can afford to hold, possibly because he controls their access to certain camps and certain shows and possibly because his version is easier to hold than her version, which requires them to have been in proximity to something they did not see and should have seen.

The two who stayed have been checking in. One sends a voice note every three days — not asking for a report, not asking her to explain anything, just: “Hey, I’ve been thinking about you. I hope you ate something good today. I don’t need you to respond.” The other shows up physically, which is the act that costs the most and means the most, with soup sometimes and sometimes just her presence, sitting in the apartment that has the gray ceiling.

The soup is very good. It is cream of tomato. It comes from a can but she heats it properly, with milk, not water, which is the sign of someone who takes soup seriously.

She is eating the soup at three twenty-six in the morning, having abandoned the project of sleeping, sitting on the couch with the bowl in her lap, and she is thinking about what it means that “she heated the soup with milk, not water” is one of the more comforting facts she has available right now.

Not the only comforting fact. Just: one of them.

She has been doing the things.

The things are: texting the crisis line three times since the festival, which connects her to someone who is calm and unhurried in the way of people specifically trained to be calm and unhurried at three a.m. and which has, each time, helped the encore run down faster. Finding the RAINN hotline number and putting it in her phone as a contact under “resources” in the same note as the Zendo number and the SMART Recovery number and the number for the local DV advocacy organization and the NAMI helpline. Not because she is certain any of them are right for her situation specifically, but because having them in the phone at three a.m. means the research was done at noon and noon-brain is a better researcher than three-a.m.-brain.

She has been doing the re-entry wobble work, which is not a clinical term for anything, just the name she has given to the specific practice of being in the gray apartment without making the gray apartment a verdict on her whole life. The gray apartment is a gray apartment. It is not evidence of failure. It is where she lives right now while the other thing resolves. The other thing resolving has a timeline that is not three weeks. She knows this.

She knows this because she found a blog post by someone who had been in a similar situation who said: “The timeline for the nervous system to recalibrate after a high-control relationship that operated through your scene identity is longer than three weeks. It is longer than three months. There is no shame in this. It is the neurology of what happened, not the measure of your resilience.”

She saved the blog post.

She re-reads it at three a.m. sometimes.

The soup is warm.

The ceiling is the ceiling.

The encore is not the truth.

She is going to go back to sleep.

🎚️

THE SOUNDBOARD QUOTE

“The encore runs because it was installed, not because it’s accurate. Your job at three a.m. is not to argue with the voice. Your job is to notice it’s his voice wearing your voice’s clothes and to say: ‘Not tonight.’ You don’t have to win the argument. You have to survive until the therapist appointment. You have to eat the soup. You have to make it to nine a.m. After nine a.m., you get more tools. At three a.m., you just have to make it to nine.”

— Mara “Hot Water” Delgado, forty-seven. Third and final appearance. The PLURth Angel’s harm-reduction auntie, the person who sits with people in the good moment and in the long after. Has developed, over seventeen years of sitting with the long after, a specific and non-negotiable set of three a.m. operating instructions that she distributes freely and recites on request. Has also developed a very good soup recipe, which she distributes with the same frequency and equal conviction. Recorded at a mutual aid meeting in Asheville, wearing the vest with seven patches and a tired expression that is not despair but the specific quality of someone who has seen everything and is still choosing to show up, which is different.
